The movement of people speaking Indo-Aryan languages from Central Asia into northwest South Asia, probably starting after 2000 BCE and going on for centuries. Their speech is the ancestor of most languages of north India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka today, including Hindi, Urdu, Bengali and Punjabi.

It was not a single invasion. It was a slow spread of small groups during the late Harappan period, as the Indus cities declined, followed by a shift of language across the north of the subcontinent.

The newcomers' ancestors lived on the steppe north of the Caspian and Aral seas, in the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures, and before that in the world of the Yamnaya herders. They probably passed through Bactria and Margiana, in today's Turkmenistan and Afghanistan. Close cousins went west to Iran and spoke Iranian languages. Another branch turns up in the Mitanni kingdom of Syria, whose treaties around 1380 BCE name the gods Mitra, Varuna and Indra.

They brought the domesticated horse, spoke-wheeled chariots and the religion of the Rigveda. The evidence is linguistic, textual and, since about 2018, genetic: ancient DNA shows steppe ancestry entering South Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE.

The topic is politically charged in India, where some argue that Indo-Aryan languages began in India and spread outward. Most linguists and geneticists support migration into India.
